docs.title: ipyllm
docs.text:
ipyllm is an IPython extension for discussing your live Python session with models supported by the llm package. Ask questions about your variables or REPL history, request plots, and have the model run code in the active IPython shell. It also works inside a live script: drop a debugging session with IPython.embed() and load ipyllm to bring a coding assistant into that function's local scope.

Start with the installation guide, then see usage and commands.

Code runs with your permissions

Model-requested code executes in the live Python process. It is not sandboxed and can access files, the network, and session objects. Enable approval when you want to review code before execution; approval is not a security boundary.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Install ipyllm into the same Python environment used by IPython:

python -m pip install .

Run that command from the project checkout. The project requires Python 3.14 or newer.

docs.title: Configure a model
docs.text:
ipyllm uses the model and provider configuration managed by llm. Configure a provider key, then choose a default model:

llm keys set PROVIDER
llm models
llm models default MODEL

For local Ollama models, the llm-ollama plugin is included. Install and start Ollama, then select an installed model with llm models default MODEL.

docs.title: Install remote provider support
docs.text:
The optional providers dependency group installs plugins for Anthropic, DeepSeek, Gemini, Grok, Mistral, OpenRouter, and Perplexity. In a checkout of this project, install the group and run IPython in the resulting environment:

uv sync --group providers
uv run ipython

uv run uses the project environment, so you do not need to activate it manually. If you prefer an activated shell, use source .venv/bin/activate on macOS/Linux or .venv\Scripts\activate on Windows, then run ipython.

The group installs these plugins: llm-anthropic, llm-deepseek, llm-gemini, llm-grok, llm-mistral, llm-openrouter, and llm-perplexity. If you installed ipyllm into another environment rather than syncing this checkout, install the plugin package(s) you need into that same environment, for example:

python -m pip install llm-anthropic llm-gemini

Configure credentials for each provider using the key name documented by its plugin. You can store a key with llm keys set PROVIDER, or set the provider's documented environment variable in the shell before starting IPython. For example, llm keys set anthropic stores an Anthropic key; environment variables must be available to the IPython process.

Then list available models and choose one:

llm models
llm models default MODEL

See the llm remote API plugin directory for the supported providers and links to plugin-specific setup instructions. The llm API key guide covers stored keys and environment variables.

docs.title: Load the extension
docs.text:
Start IPython or a Jupyter IPython kernel from the configured environment and load the extension:

%load_ext ipyllm

To load it automatically each time IPython starts, add this to the profile's ipython_config.py:

c.InteractiveShellApp.extensions = ["ipyllm"]

See the IPython configuration guide for profile locations and configuration details.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Use %llm for a single-line prompt or %%llm for a multi-line prompt:

%llm What variables are available? Explain `data`.

%%llm
Plot the time series in `data` with matplotlib and run the plotting code.

The conversation stays in memory for the current IPython session. The model starts with variable names and Python types only, and can request additional context through tools:

  • list_variables lists visible names and types.
  • inspect_variable returns a bounded representation of one variable.
  • get_history reads recent inputs, or a requested IPython history range such as 1-5.
  • execute_code runs code in the active shell, allowing it to use live objects and display plots.

docs.title: Diagnose a shell command
docs.text:
Run a command inside %%llm --run to capture its output and ask the model for help understanding the result:

%%llm --run Explain the likely cause and suggest a fix.
pytest -q

The command runs locally in a shell. ipyllm displays its stdout, stderr, and exit status, then sends the captured output and your diagnostic request to the current model conversation. If you omit the request, it asks for a diagnosis and suggestions without rerunning the command:

%%llm --run
python -m pip check

This is opt-in; normal REPL output is not captured or sent automatically. Output is limited to 12,000 characters in the model prompt (keeping the beginning and end), and commands time out after 120 seconds by default. Change the timeout in ipython_config.py with c.IpyllmMagics.command_timeout = 60.

Only run commands you intended to execute. Command output may contain credentials, private paths, or other sensitive data; review it and your model provider's data handling before sending it.

docs.title: Debug in a live script with IPython.embed
docs.text:
Drop a debugging session into any point of a running script and get a coding assistant with access to the function's live local variables:

from IPython import embed

def process(rows):
    result = heavy_computation(rows)
    if result is None:
        from IPython import embed
        embed()  # inspect `rows` and `result` interactively
    return result

Inside the embedded shell, load ipyllm and it sees the surrounding function's local variables:

%load_ext ipyllm
%llm What is holding `result` in a None state? Suggest how to fix the logic above.

Because embed() runs in the same process and frame, ipyllm's tools (list_variables, inspect_variable, get_history, execute_code) operate directly on the local names at that point in the code. You can ask the model to trace how an unexpected value was produced, check state of earlier variables, or run fix-and-retry experiments on the live objects before continuing.

The usual caveats apply: embedded code is not sandboxed, and anything you ask the model to inspect or execute has the same permissions as the running process.

docs.title: Use Agent Skills
docs.text:
ipyllm can load local Agent Skills as task instructions. Each skill is a directory containing a SKILL.md with YAML frontmatter (name and description) followed by Markdown instructions.

By default, skills are discovered in project- and user-level directories named .agents/skills/, .claude/skills/, .github/skills/, .cursor/skills/, and .windsurf/skills/. List available skills and descriptions with:

%llm --skills

Select a skill explicitly as the first prompt token. This works for both line and cell prompts:

%llm /pandas Find and fix the missing values in `data`.

%%llm /seaborn
Compare the distributions in `data` and explain the plot.

Only the selected SKILL.md instructions are added to that turn's prompt; other skills are not loaded into the conversation. The skill guides the model and does not run its scripts or grant new tools. Skills are local text and should be reviewed like any other prompt context.

Add extra skill directories in the IPython profile's ipython_config.py:

c.IpyllmMagics.skill_paths = [
    "~/my-skills",
    "./team/skills",
]

Relative paths are resolved from the current working directory. If two discovered skills use the same name, invocation is rejected as ambiguous. Malformed skill metadata and missing configured directories are reported by %llm --skills. Skill instruction files larger than 32,000 characters are rejected.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Command Purpose %llm --model MODEL Select a model for this session; starts a fresh conversation. %llm --approval on Ask before executing code requested by the model. %llm --approval off Execute model-requested code without an approval prompt. %llm --skills List discovered skills and descriptions. %llm --config Show the effective model and approval setting. %llm --reset Clear the current conversation.

Code execution is automatic by default. To require approval by default, add these settings to the IPython profile's ipython_config.py:

c.IpyllmMagics.require_approval = True
c.IpyllmMagics.model = "MODEL"

Session commands %llm --approval ... and %llm --model ... override the profile settings for the current shell. The approval prompt requires the exact response yes.

Execution is not sandboxed

Executed code has the same permissions as the IPython process. It can read or modify files, use the network, and change session objects. Approval is a review step, not a security boundary. Use trusted models/providers and do not expose secrets to a provider that should not receive them.
